title: Julia tutorial: arrays, functions, multiple dispatch and packages — cv.cm
description: Learn Julia from scratch: install with juliaup, run Hello world, use types, 1-based arrays, broadcasting, functions, multiple dispatch, errors and packages.
answer: Julia is a high-level, dynamically typed language designed for fast numerical and scientific computing. It reads like Python or MATLAB but compiles each function to native code the first time it is called, so loops can run at speeds close to C. Its central idea is multiple dispatch: a function picks its method based on the types of all its arguments. Install it with juliaup and run a file with `julia hello.jl`.

sections.h: What Julia is and who uses it
body: Julia was created by Jeff Bezanson, Stefan Karpinski, Viral Shah and Alan Edelman, and it became public in 2012. Version 1.0 arrived in 2018, and the 1.x series keeps backward compatibility. Julia aims to solve the "two-language problem": prototyping in a slow, easy language and then rewriting the hot parts in C or Fortran.

Julia is used by scientists, engineers and data analysts for simulation, differential equations, optimization, statistics, machine learning and high-performance computing. Its package ecosystem covers data frames, plotting, GPU computing and automatic differentiation.

sections.h: Install Julia and run Hello, world
body: The recommended installer is juliaup, which installs and updates Julia versions on Windows, macOS and Linux (see julialang.org/downloads). After installation, `julia` starts the REPL and `julia file.jl` runs a script.

body.code:
julia hello.jl
# Hello, world!
julia
# julia> 1 + 2
# 3

body: In the REPL, press `]` to enter package mode (for example `add DataFrames`), `?` for help on a name, and `;` for a shell. Press Backspace to return to the normal prompt.
Variables need no declaration, but every value has a concrete type, which you can inspect with `typeof`. You can add type annotations to function arguments and struct fields when you want them.

head: Type
Example
Notes
rows: Default integer on 64-bit systems; overflow wraps around
An interned name, often used as a key or option
"No value", returned by functions with no result

body.code:
name = "Ana"
age = 30
println("$name is $age, next year $(age + 1)")
# Ana is 30, next year 31
typeof(age)   # Int64
7 / 2         # 3.5  (always a float)
7 ÷ 2         # 3    (integer division, also div(7, 2))
2^10          # 1024

body: Julia accepts Unicode names such as `π` or `α`; in the REPL and most editors you type `\pi` and press Tab to get `π`.
Blocks end with the keyword `end`; indentation is for readability only. `if`, `for` and `while` work as in most languages, and comprehensions build arrays in one line.

body.code:
function sign_name(n)
    if n > 0
        "positive"
    elseif n < 0
        "negative"
    else
        "zero"
    end
end
for i in 1:3
    println("$i squared is $(i^2)")
end
squares = [x^2 for x in 1:5 if isodd(x)]   # [1, 9, 25]
x = 5
result = x > 3 ? "big" : "small"           # "big"

body: `1:3` is a range that includes both ends. The last expression in a function or `if` block is its value, so `sign_name(-2)` returns `"negative"` without an explicit `return`.

body.code:
add(x, y) = x + y                 # one-line definition
function greet(name = "world"; punctuation = "!")
    return "Hello, $name$punctuation"
end
greet()                           # "Hello, world!"
greet("Ana", punctuation = ".")   # "Hello, Ana."
square = x -> x^2                 # anonymous function
map(square, [1, 2, 3])            # [1, 4, 9]
v = [3, 1, 2]
sort!(v)                          # v is now [1, 2, 3]

body: Positional arguments come before the semicolon and keyword arguments after it. By convention, a function whose name ends in `!` modifies one of its arguments, such as `sort!` or `push!`, while `sort` returns a new array.
The dot syntax is called broadcasting: `f.(x)` applies `f` to every element, and `.+`, `.*` work element by element. Julia fuses chains of dotted operations into a single loop.

A Julia function can have many methods. When you call it, Julia chooses the most specific method for the types of all the arguments. This replaces class methods: types hold data, and behavior is added by defining methods for them, even from another package.

body.code:
abstract type Shape end
struct Circle <: Shape
    r::Float64
end
struct Rect <: Shape
    w::Float64
    h::Float64
end
area(c::Circle) = π * c.r^2
area(r::Rect) = r.w * r.h
shapes = [Circle(1.0), Rect(2.0, 3.0)]
println(round.(area.(shapes), digits = 2))   # [3.14, 6.0]

body: Because Julia compiles a specialized version of a function for the argument types it sees, the first call of a function is slower (it includes compilation) and later calls are fast. Use `mutable struct` when fields must change after creation.

Julia uses exceptions. Throw a built-in exception type such as `ArgumentError` or `DomainError`, or define your own as a struct that subtypes `Exception`. `tryparse` returns `nothing` instead of throwing.

body.code:
function parse_age(s)
    n = tryparse(Int, s)
    n === nothing && throw(ArgumentError("not a number: $s"))
    n < 0 && throw(DomainError(n, "age must not be negative"))
    return n
end
try
    parse_age("abc")
catch e
    if e isa ArgumentError
        println("Error: ", e.msg)
    else
        rethrow()
    end
end
# Error: not a number: abc

sections.h: A small complete program: word frequencies

body.code:
text = "the cat and the hat and the bat"
counts = Dict{String,Int}()
for w in split(text)
    counts[w] = get(counts, w, 0) + 1
end
top = sort(collect(counts), by = last, rev = true)
for (word, n) in first(top, 2)
    println(word, " ", n)
end
# the 3
# and 2

body: `split` breaks the string on whitespace, `get` returns a default of 0 for new words, `collect` turns the dictionary into a vector of `word => count` pairs, and `by = last` sorts by the count.

body.note: Common beginner mistakes: indexing from 0 (`v[0]` is an error; the first element is `v[1]`); expecting `7 / 2` to be an integer; writing performance-critical code at the top level of a script instead of inside functions (global variables are slow, and assigning a global inside a top-level loop in a file triggers a scope warning); and timing only the first call, which includes compilation.

faq.a: For code with many loops and numeric work, Julia is usually much faster than pure Python because it compiles to native code. Python with libraries such as NumPy can be fast for vectorized operations, so the difference depends on the task.

faq.q: Why does Julia start counting at 1?
faq.a: Julia follows the convention of mathematics and of languages such as MATLAB, R and Fortran, where the first element of an array has index 1.

faq.q: Why is the first run of my Julia code slow?
faq.a: Julia compiles each function for the argument types the first time it is called. Later calls reuse the compiled code, so measure performance after a warm-up call or with a benchmarking package.
